extracted.intended_audience: regulated entities, industry stakeholders, state regulators, and commenters on the EPA's GHG rule for steam generating units (power plant owners/operators, pipeline developers, environmental lawyers, and policy analysts)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation of whether carbon capture, transport, and storage (CCS) — including 90% CO2 capture at coal-fired steam generating units and associated CO2 pipeline transport — is adequately demonstrated for purposes of the EPA's BSER determination in a federal rulemaking. Covers technical performance, demonstrations, transport logistics, permitting, and supporting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: State CCS Requirements as evidence of CCS maturity
rubrics_metrics.description: Several states encourage or require sources to install CCS; these state requirements further indicate that CCS is well-established and effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites statutes and plans (e.g., Illinois Climate and Equitable Jobs Act requiring zero emissions by certain dates and CCS-based standards since 2009 with capture rate requirements rising to 90%; Michigan's 80% by 2035 and 100% by 2040 with 90% capture qualifying as 'clean energy'; California scoping plan and Assembly Bill 1279 requiring planning and policies to enable CCS; Louisiana, Pennsylvania, North Dakota, Wyoming strategic planning and laws). Use of state requirements and plans as supporting evidence that CCS is deployed, encouraged, and feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable load and startup/shutdown impacts on achievable capture
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether variable load, turndown, and startup/shutdown conditions prevent achieving 90% CO2 capture over long periods (i.e., a year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points: coal EGUs typically turndown to ~40% of design capacity and have high duty cycles (avg ~70%); demonstrated capture plant turndowns of ~60–70% (Boundary Dam, Petra Nova); single capture train turndown to 50% achievable, two trains allow turndown to 25%; capture efficiencies often increase at lower throughputs (example: solvent/design achieving 90% at full load reached 97.5% at 62.5% net load); startups/shutdowns are infrequent and have low heat input, often use lower-carbon fuels, so their contribution to annual emissions is small; tax incentives (IRC §45Q) provide operational incentives to run at higher capacity factors. Conclusion: variable load and startups/shutdowns do not generally affect achievability of 90% capture over a year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Achievability across coal ranks
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether 90% CO2 capture is achievable for all coal ranks (lignite, subbituminous, bituminous, anthracite, waste coal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: amine solvents have been used across a broad range of flue gas compositions and coal ranks; CO2 concentration differences are slight (generally 13–15% for coal combustion flue gas) and can be accommodated by design and absorber sizing; impurities (SO2, NOx, PM, trace contaminants) can be managed with existing pre-conditioning controls (FGD for SO2, polishing columns, solvent reclaiming with activated carbon beds); EPA included costs of adding FGD where needed. Demonstrations cited: Boundary Dam (lignite), Milton R. Young pilot tests, W.A. Parish (subbituminous), Plant Barry, Warrior Run, Argus Cogeneration (bituminous), Wilhelmshaven (anthracite), Shady Point. Conclusion: 90% capture is achievable across coal ranks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of NG turbine CO2 capture experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Use experience from CO2 capture on natural gas-fired combustion turbines to support achievability for coal-fired steam generating units (and vice versa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes information about CO2 capture from NG turbines (described elsewhere in the preamble) and states that lessons and data are transferable between NG turbines and coal-fired units, providing additional support for the 90% capture determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of non-EPAct05 evidence to demonstrate 90% capture
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether evidence excluding EPAct05-assisted projects is sufficient to find 90% capture adequately demonstrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's conservative legal approach: cannot rely solely on EPAct05-assisted projects but may use them to corroborate other evidence. Sets out the package of non-EPAct05 information the Agency finds sufficient: Boundary Dam plus engineering analyses of improvements; other coal-fired demonstrations (Argus, Warrior Run); industrial CCS applications; vendor statements; NG turbine capture experience (excluding EPAct05-assisted projects). EPAct05-assisted projects provide additional confirmation but are not required as the sole basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: CO2 transport by pipeline adequately demonstrated
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether CO2 transport by pipelines, as a component of CCS, is adequately demonstrated and feasible for power plants to access storage reservoirs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA finalizes determination that pipeline transport is adequately demonstrated. PHMSA is updating safety regs. For BSER analysis EPA conservatively premises transport on construction of relatively short lateral pipelines from source to nearest geological storage (deep saline formations, unmineable coal seams, depleted reservoirs) rather than assuming a large interstate trunkline network. Most coal EGUs are relatively close to potential storage; majority within short distances (see distance metrics). EPA believes new and existing EGUs are capable of constructing necessary pipelines and has assurances of safety via PHMSA regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance/proximity of sources to sequestration sites and projected pipeline lengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider geographic availability of storage (deep saline formations etc.) and resulting pipeline-mileage requirements to determine feasibility and cost assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data: >50% of coal capacity within 20 miles (32 km) of potential saline sites; 73% within 31 miles (50 km); 80% within 62 miles (100 km); 91% within 100 miles (160 km). In GW terms, of 81 GW planned to operate after 2039, only 16 GW not within 100 km, 7 GW not within 160 km. EPA projects ~8,000 km (5,000 miles) of CO2 pipelines would be required by 2032 under a scenario where each plant builds a lateral to nearest saline site (not optimized). Compliance modeling projects 3,300 miles baseline and 4,700 miles in policy scenario; annual average 660–940 miles/year. Comparison: historical natural gas pipeline construction ranged 1,000–2,500 miles/year (2017–2021), so projected CO2 pipeline buildout is within observed pipeline construction capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical CO2 pipeline projects as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use prior CO2 pipeline projects (lengths, capacities, purposes) to demonstrate that CO2 pipeline design, construction, and operation have been adequately demonstrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA reported 8,666 km (5,385 miles) of CO2 pipelines in operation in 2022 (14% increase since 2011). Examples: Beaver Creek (76 km), Monell (52.6 km), Bairoil (258 km), Cortez (808 km), Sheep Mountain (656 km), etc.; capacities from 1.6 to 27 million tons/year; uses include EOR. Specific U.S. project examples: 109 km Coffeyville->North Burbank (fertilizer to EOR), 132 km Terrell Gas to Permian Basin, 96 km Kemper County (IGCC to EOR), 19 km Citronelle to saline storage. These demonstrate varied lengths, capacities, purposes, and successful construction/operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of EPAct05-assisted CO2 pipelines in supporting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider EPAct05-funded pipeline projects as corroborating information but not the sole basis for adequacy when EPA's legal interpretation restricts sole reliance on such projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPAct05-funded projects that built pipelines include Illinois Industrial Carbon Capture, Petra Nova (131 km pipeline), Red Trail Energy, and Project Tundra (0.4 km). EPA may rely on these projects to corroborate other sources of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and planning of CO2 trunklines and hubs
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how existing and planned trunklines/hubs could affect miles of new pipeline required and cost estimates, while noting BSER does not assume trunkline buildout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maps of existing/planned pipelines and storage appear in TSD. Major planned projects (e.g., Summit Carbon Solutions Midwest Carbon Express ~3,200 km, Wolf Carbon Solutions Mt. Simon Hub expansion, Tallgrass converting 630 km NG pipeline) could reduce miles individual plants must build. EPA's analysis is conservative and does not assume trunkline buildout; trunklines would lower costs and provide more options but are not required for the BSER conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitting, rights-of-way, and eminent domain considerations for CO2 pipelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess permitting complexity and rights-of-way acquisition as factors in feasibility of CO2 pipeline construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting involves private, local, state, tribal, and federal agencies; state laws govern siting, rights-of-way, and eminent domain (varies by state). Some states treat CO2 pipeline operators as common carriers/public utilities and explicitly permit eminent domain (17 states). Interstate pipelines typically involve multiple state agencies and longer permitting timelines; intrastate pipelines typically involve a single primary state regulator. States have developed streamlined/joint permitting forms (Illinois, Louisiana, New York, Pennsylvania). Rights-of-way acquisition examples: Summit Carbon Solutions easement agreements with thousands of landowners and high percentages of rights-of-way acquired in several states; Citronelle acquired rights across challenging habitats. Demonstrated ability to secure rights-of-way across private, state, and federal lands (example: Denbury Cedar Creek pipeline crossed state school trust lands and federal lands).

rubrics_metrics.name: NEPA and federal review timelines and requirements for pipeline projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether federal funding or actions trigger NEPA review (EA or EIS) and how NEPA timelines affect project feasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal actions (e.g., funding a CCS project) generally require NEPA compliance. EA determines whether significant effects exist; EIS required if significant effects anticipated. Level of review depends on whole-project impacts (habitats, cultural resources, wetlands, public safety, crossings of waters). Fiscal Responsibility Act amendments set deadlines: EA within 1 year, EIS within 2 years (lead agency may extend in consultation with applicant only as necessary). Examples: ADM Decatur pipeline (1.9 km) required only an EA; Petra Nova (131 km) required an EIS (DOE funding) with record of decision issued in under 2 years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative feasibility: CO2 pipeline buildout vs other pipeline construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare projected CO2 pipeline annual mileage with historical pipeline construction (e.g., natural gas) to assess feasibility of rapid buildout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA projects 660–940 miles/year average for CO2 pipeline capacity in the buildout scenario — less than historic annual natural gas pipeline construction (roughly 1,000–2,500 miles/year in 2017–2021). This comparison supports the conclusion that projected CO2 pipeline construction is feasible within existing U.S. pipeline construction capacity.
